# Shipped agent-type profiles.
#
# Each top-level table is one `tool_type` - the string an `agent_tools` row
# stores to say what kind of agent a config launches. This file is compiled
# into the binary (`include_str!`) and is the authoritative default set; a user
# override at `<config-dir>/panopt/agent-types.toml` is merged on top (scalars
# override, maps merge by inner key, lists replace wholesale). See
# `panopt-core::agent_profiles` for the merge rule, the placeholder set, and
# load-time validation.
#
# A profile is pure data driving generic interpreters: `spawn` is a template the
# spawn interpreter renders into a concrete (argv, env, files) launch; `status`
# is regexes the status interpreter matches against the agent's output. There is
# no per-type code - adding an agent type that fits this shape is a new table
# here (or in the override), not a code change.

[claude-code]
display_name = "Claude Code"

[claude-code.spawn]
# Launch claude with a generated stdio MCP config that boots `panopt _mcp-proxy`.
# The proxy holds the long-lived MCP session and forwards to panoptd over HTTP,
# so the session survives daemon restarts. This mirrors the cockpit's
# hand-built launch (crates/panopt/src/mcp.rs) - except panopt renders the
# `{{...}}` placeholders itself rather than leaning on claude's own `${VAR}`
# expansion, which is what lets the same engine launch agents that don't expand
# env vars.
argv = ["claude", "--mcp-config", "{{file:mcp_config}}"]

[claude-code.spawn.files]
# Rendered to a temp file at spawn; its path replaces `{{file:mcp_config}}` in
# argv. A multi-line TOML literal string ('''...''') holds the JSON verbatim.
mcp_config = '''
{
  "mcpServers": {
    "panopt": {
      "type": "stdio",
      "command": "{{panopt_bin}}",
      "args": [
        "--port", "{{port}}",
        "_mcp-proxy",
        "--host", "{{host}}",
        "--ws", "{{ws}}",
        "--project", "{{project}}",
        "--id", "{{agent_id}}",
        "--name", "{{name}}",
        "--token", "{{token}}"
      ]
    }
  }
}
'''

[claude-code.status]
# Regexes matched against the agent's terminal output to derive its activity.
# PROVISIONAL: the interpreter semantics (precedence, idle fallthrough) and the
# fixture-validated patterns land in #138; this file only declares the shape so
# the schema and loader have real data to exercise. Lists replace wholesale on
# override.
thinking = ['esc to interrupt']
waiting = ['Do you want', 'Would you like']

### 6.6 Agent tools and processes

PANopt splits a project's launchable agents and commands across two tables, a
config layer and an instance layer, mirroring Solo's two-layer model:

- **`agent_tools`** - durable per-project configurations: name, command, cwd,
  a `tool_type` that names an agent-type profile (Section 6.7), and an
  `enabled` flag controlling whether the config is offered in spawn UIs. One
  tool can back many running instances. Because the profile registry lives in
  a file, not a table, `tool_type` cannot be a SQL foreign key; it is validated
  at the application layer (`Store::agent_tool_create`/`_update` reject a key
  with no profile), and a row left referencing a since-removed profile is
  flagged in the UI rather than hard-failing.
- **`processes`** - per-project instances of an agent, command, or terminal:
  `kind` (`agent` / `command` / `terminal`), name, command, cwd, an optional
  `agent_tool_id` back-reference, plus nullable lifecycle columns (`pid`,
  `status`, `agent_state`, `last_seen`).

A `processes` row's columns divide into two roles - a spec/status split. The
**desired** (spec) columns are copied from the source config at spawn - `kind`,
`name`, `command`, `cwd`, and the `agent_tool_id` back-reference - and a later
edit to the tool does not perturb them. The **runtime** (status) columns -
`pid`, `status`, `agent_state`, `last_seen` - are written by the lifecycle
layer while the instance runs and are NULL when it is not. The config is what
*should* run; the row's runtime columns are what *is* running; the two may
legitimately diverge (edited-but-not-restarted, crashed, never-started). This is
why config and instance stay distinct even at today's one-instance-per-config:
run-level identity is where a session or plan attaches, not the durable slot.

The split lets a project carry two Claude instances both spawned from agent
tool `#3`, with each instance addressable by its own `#N`. When a process is
spawned from a tool, the tool's `command` and `cwd` are copied into the
process row so post-spawn edits to the tool don't perturb the running
instance. Deleting a tool nulls the `agent_tool_id` back-reference on any
process that referenced it; the live instance keeps running.

Both tables draw ids from the unified per-project `next_id` counter
(Section 6.4), so a `#N` reference still resolves to exactly one row across
todos, notes, agent_tools, and processes.

Whether a process is currently running is *not* stored today: the cockpit
derives it from live Zellij pane state, same as the pre-V6 roster did. The
nullable lifecycle columns turn that into a follow-up rather than a schema
break, once panoptd owns process spawn (Section 10).

The config and instance layers each project to their own markdown file:
`.panopt/agent_tools.md` and `.panopt/processes.md`. The cockpit sidebar
currently renders only `processes.md`, because it is a live-state view;
agent_tools render once a spawn UI lands.

Both layers are distinct from the agent registry (Section 6.3): the registry
is the ephemeral set of MCP agents *currently connected*, while agent_tools
and processes are the durable set of agents/commands/terminals the project
is configured to run and the live instances of them.

581	`codex`, ...); the profile for that type holds everything needed to *interop*
582	with that specific agent program. Crucially, a type is **data, not code**: a
583	profile parameterizes two generic interpreters rather than carrying a bespoke
584	adapter.
585	
586	- **spawn** - a launch template: an `argv` vector, an `env` map, and a set of
587	  `files` to materialize, all carrying `{{placeholder}}` references. The spawn
588	  interpreter renders these against the facts PANopt supplies (`panopt_bin`,
589	  `host`, `port`, `ws`, `project`, `agent_id`, `name`, `token`, `model`) into a
590	  concrete process launch. env-vs-flag-vs-config-file is not three mechanisms
591	  but one template shape - *where a placeholder lands* - so one engine launches
592	  every CLI agent. This is what lets PANopt render the launch itself rather than
593	  leaning on the agent's own `${VAR}` expansion (which the cockpit's hand-built
594	  claude config currently does; see `crates/panopt/src/mcp.rs`).
595	- **status** - regexes per activity state (`thinking` / `idle` / `waiting` /
596	  `done`) matched against the agent's output by the status interpreter.
597	
598	The only irreducible code is the interpreters themselves (substitution, pattern
599	matching) and the providers that produce the injectable facts - both fixed and
600	generic, never per-type. A genuinely novel agent (a different launch handshake,
601	a non-screen-scraped status source) needs a new interpreter *step kind*, but
602	that step then becomes declarable data for every type after it.
603	
604	Profiles are global and live in files, not SQLite: they are referenced by a
605	`tool_type` *string*, not addressed as a `#N` resource, so keeping them out of
606	the database preserves the unified per-project id invariant (Section 6.4). Two
607	layers merge, both global: shipped defaults compiled into the binary
608	(`crates/panopt-core/src/agent_profiles/defaults.toml`, where claude-code
609	lives) and a user override at `<config-dir>/panopt/agent-types.toml`, absent by
610	default. The merge is keyed by `tool_type`; within a profile, scalars override,
611	maps (`env`, `files`, status patterns) merge by inner key, and lists (`argv`,
612	each pattern list) replace wholesale. Every placeholder is validated at load -
613	a `{{name}}` outside the known set, or a `{{file:NAME}}` with no matching
614	`files` entry, fails the daemon at startup rather than at spawn time.

619	risk of its layer.

624	their shared state appears live as files.

626	Built: `panopt-core` (state and filesystem projection, no protocol
627	dependencies) and `panoptd` (an MCP server over Streamable HTTP, built on
628	`rmcp`, `tokio`, and `axum`). In-memory state behind a `Mutex`, one-way
629	projection - no SQLite yet. Seven tools: `note_create`, `note_list`,
630	`note_append`, `note_read`, `todo_create`, `todo_list`,
631	`todo_complete` (`note_create` and `note_list` were added to the
632	original five: notes are id-keyed, so a create tool mints ids and a list

637	an editor live-reloading a projected file the instant the daemon rewrites it,
638	confirmed on macOS with Zed, no prompt and no flicker.

that step then becomes declarable data for every type after it.

Profiles are global and live in files, not SQLite: they are referenced by a
`tool_type` *string*, not addressed as a `#N` resource, so keeping them out of
the database preserves the unified per-project id invariant (Section 6.4). Two
layers merge, both global: shipped defaults compiled into the binary
(`crates/panopt-core/src/agent_profiles/defaults.toml`, where claude-code
lives) and a user override at `<config-dir>/panopt/agent-types.toml`, absent by
default. The merge is keyed by `tool_type`; within a profile, scalars override,
maps (`env`, `files`, status patterns) merge by inner key, and lists (`argv`,
each pattern list) replace wholesale. Every placeholder is validated at load -
a `{{name}}` outside the known set, or a `{{file:NAME}}` with no matching
`files` entry, fails the daemon at startup rather than at spawn time.

## 7. Proof of Concept

Two proofs of concept were built and verified, each retiring the load-bearing
risk of its layer.

### 7.1 POC 1 - the coordination daemon

Goal: prove that multiple agents coordinate through one shared daemon and that
their shared state appears live as files.

Built: `panopt-core` (state and filesystem projection, no protocol
dependencies) and `panoptd` (an MCP server over Streamable HTTP, built on
`rmcp`, `tokio`, and `axum`). In-memory state behind a `Mutex`, one-way
projection - no SQLite yet. Seven tools: `note_create`, `note_list`,
`note_append`, `note_read`, `todo_create`, `todo_list`,
`todo_complete` (`note_create` and `note_list` were added to the
original five: notes are id-keyed, so a create tool mints ids and a list
tool discovers them).

Verified: two agents coordinating through a single daemon over MCP; every
mutation projected atomically to `.panopt/*.md`; and the load-bearing check -
an editor live-reloading a projected file the instant the daemon rewrites it,
confirmed on macOS with Zed, no prompt and no flicker.

  does not scale to a large Rust/Tauri GUI. Use dynamic observation instead.

  developing, turning every upstream improvement into a merge conflict.

  panel. Superseded by Zellij; see Section 4.6.

input.new_string:
## 10. Agent orchestration surface

Beyond the human cockpit, an orchestrator *agent* needs a programmatic way to
spawn, bootstrap, task, and dispose of sub-agents - the parity target is Solo's
`spawn_agent` / `send_input` / `close_process`. This rides the same
daemon-decides / plugin-effects seam as the instance lifecycle: the daemon owns
the record, the cockpit reconciles it into panes.

- **Spawn** - `spawn_agent` is a thin alias over `process_start` (same args,
  same one-live-instance-per-config policy, same dispatch path). Its return
  carries the new `process_id`, the resolved instance `name`, and rendered
  `agent_instructions` - the per-type bootstrap text (Section 6.7) the parent
  prepends to the child's first prompt. Per-launch `name` / `extra_args` vary a
  launch without mutating the config (copy-on-spawn, Section 6.6).
- **Input** - `send_input(process_id, input)`, the linchpin that turns a spawned
  child into a working one with no human keystroke: the daemon enqueues the
  input, the plugin writes it into the owned pane (`write_chars_to_pane_id`).
- **Dispose** - no new tool: Solo's `close_process` maps onto the existing
  `process_stop` (kill the process; the pane stands, per the never-close-panes
  invariant) followed by `process_delete`.

`project_id` cross-project spawn is a deferred non-goal - it collides with the
per-connection `?ws=` project scoping; revisit when a real cross-project
orchestration case appears.

## 11. Out of Scope and Future Work

- The remainder of Solo's large tool surface (timers, prompt templates,
  services). Added incrementally after the POC.
- Process spawning and supervision. Solo spawns and manages processes itself;
  PANopt initially relies on Zellij to host agent and command panes, and may
  add direct process management later.

content.text:
I have the smoking gun. Here's the investigation.

## Root cause: the proxy throws away panopt's MCP `instructions`

Agents connect to panopt through `panopt _mcp-proxy` (the stdio MCP server baked into every agent's launch config). The proxy is its **own** MCP server from Claude Code's perspective, and it answers `initialize` locally instead of forwarding panopt's:

- `crates/panopt/src/mcp_proxy.rs:204` — `handle_initialize` returns a hardcoded result with `protocolVersion`, `capabilities`, `serverInfo` — **and no `instructions` field at all.**
- `crates/panopt/src/mcp_proxy.rs:292` — when the proxy initializes its *own* session against panoptd, it receives panoptd's full response (which carries the rich `with_instructions(...)` block) and does `let _ = resp.into_string(); // discard the JSON-RPC body; we only needed the header`.

So panopt writes a detailed server-instructions block (`handler.rs:1897`), the proxy fetches it, **discards it**, and hands Claude Code an initialize result with nothing in it. **The agent never sees one word of panopt's guidance.** All it gets is the forwarded `tools/list` — bare tool names + per-tool descriptions.

Claude Code ships with a built-in, heavily-reinforced `Task` sub-agent tool. With zero server-level steering from panopt, "spawn an agent" maps to the built-in. Solo's MCP server is connected directly (no stripping proxy), so Claude Code receives Solo's server instructions, which claim the "spawn an agent" verb — hence Solo wins.

## Secondary cause: even the content wouldn't steer it

Even if the instructions flowed, they don't claim the verb:
- `handler.rs:1897-1953` — the instructions describe registry/locks/todos/notes/configs/processes but **never say "to spawn or run an agent, use panopt instead of your built-in sub-agent tool."** Processes are only listed as `process_create/list/get/update/delete` — `process_start`/`spawn_agent`/`process_stop` aren't even mentioned.
- At the time of your test, the only spawn-ish tool was `process_start`, described as *"Start an instance of an agent config"* — not "spawn an agent." (`spawn_agent`, which I added in #159, isn't deployed yet and its description does say "Spawn a sub-agent" — necessary but not sufficient without the server-level framing.)

## Capability nuance (a real model difference, not just wording)

panopt's `spawn_agent`/`process_start` spawns an instance of a **pre-existing `agent_tool` config** and can't yet pass an ad-hoc task. "Spawn an agent to check the weather in Portland" has no config to spawn from and no way to hand it the task — task-passing is exactly #160 (`send_input`), which isn't built. Solo's spawn_agent takes a prompt and spins up an ephemeral agent. So fully matching Solo's behavior needs: (a) the steering fix below, **and** (b) ad-hoc/by-type spawn + #160's input channel.

## Recommended fix

1. **Stop dropping the instructions** — have the proxy surface panopt's server instructions in its `initialize` reply (forward panoptd's `instructions`, or bake a strong string into `handle_initialize`). This is the single highest-leverage change.
2. **Claim the verb in the instructions** — add an orchestration line: *"When the user asks to spawn / launch / run an agent in this project, use `spawn_agent` (NOT your built-in sub-agent/Task tool) so the agent appears in the cockpit and joins the shared coordination plane."* Mention `process_start`/`process_stop` too.
3. (Follow-on, for true parity) ad-hoc spawn + #160 `send_input` so an orchestrator can spawn *and task* a child.

Items 1–2 are small and directly produce the behavior you want. Want me to implement them now? (I'd also fold in #160 as the natural next piece for the task-passing half — but 1–2 alone fix the "it used its own sub-agent" discrepancy.)

{"id":160,"title":"Instance input channel: send_input MCP → plugin writes into the pane","body":"The tasking half of the **agent-facing orchestration surface** — deliver input (first prompt and follow-ups) to a running interactive instance. Brings panopt to parity with solo's `send_input`. The orchestration linchpin: `spawn_agent` → get `agent_instructions` → **`send_input(process_id, instructions + task)`** to actually set the child working.

## The seam (mirror of #141's spawn reconcile)
panoptd cannot touch a pane — it is a headless HTTP daemon with no terminal. So input rides the *same* daemon-decides / plugin-effects / Zellij-owns model #141 establishes, run in reverse:
1. **`send_input(process_id, input)`** (MCP) — panoptd validates the instance is `running`, then **enqueues** the input as desired state (a pending-input queue keyed by process id; the daemon owns the *intent*, never the act).
2. **The plugin drains it.** The reconcile loop (alongside `reconcile_starting_processes`, main.rs:1879) reads the pending queue on its existing poll, and writes the bytes into the pane it already owns the pane-id for (from the #141 spawn reconcile) via Zellij's `write_chars_to_pane_id`. No new push channel. Requires adding the pane-write capability to the plugin's `PermissionType` set (currently ReadApplicationState/ChangeApplicationState/RunCommands/WriteToClipboard).
3. panoptd marks the queue entry delivered.

Honors the invariant: **the daemon never touches the pane; the plugin is the sole effector**, same as spawn.

## Open questions to resolve in-todo

Done — implemented alongside the root-cause fix for why agents weren't using panopt to spawn.

**Why agents ignored panopt (investigation):** the `_mcp-proxy` answered Claude Code's `initialize` locally and dropped panoptd's server `instructions` entirely (`mcp_proxy.rs` discarded the init body, `handle_initialize` carried no instructions field). So the agent never saw any panopt guidance — only bare tool descriptions — and fell back to its built-in Task tool. Solo connects directly, so its instructions reach the client.

**Fix (3 parts):**
1. Proxy now captures panoptd's `instructions` on connect and passes them through in its local `initialize` reply (`mcp_proxy.rs`). +2 tests.
2. Instructions now claim the verb: an "Spawning and tasking agents" section tells the agent to use `spawn_agent` (NOT its built-in sub-agent tool) for in-project agents, and documents `send_input`/`process_stop` (`handler.rs`).
3. The send_input pipeline + ad-hoc spawn:

**send_input (#160), the daemon-decides/plugin-effects seam in reverse:**
- DB: `process_inputs` queue (V16 migration, global autoincrement id = order + ack key).
- Core: `send_input` (validates instance is live — `starting` or `running`; rejects stopped/unknown with a typed error), `pending_inputs`, `ack_input`; projects undelivered rows to `.panopt/.cockpit/inputs.jsonl`.
- MCP: `send_input(process_id, input)` (agent-facing) + `input_ack(seq)` (cockpit-internal).
- Plugin: `deliver_pending_inputs` (Todos-gatekeeper, each poll) reads inputs.jsonl, writes each into the owned pane via `write_chars_to_pane_id`, acks via `panopt _input-ack`. Added `PermissionType::WriteToStdin` (was missing — writes would have silently no-op'd) and a `delivered_inputs` guard against the projection-lag double-type window. JSONL parsed in panopt-zellij-logic via serde_json (host-tested).

**Ad-hoc spawn (extends #159):** `spawn_agent` now takes optional `tool_type`/`prompt`/`name`; with no `agent_tool_id` it auto-creates a config (so the agent appears in the cockpit and reuses the whole pipeline) and queues `prompt` as the opening input — so `spawn_agent(prompt="check the weather in Portland")` spawns AND tasks a child with no human keystroke.

**Resolved open questions from this todo:** submit convention = trailing newline (spawn appends one to the prompt; send_input documents that a trailing newline submits) — kept data-light, no per-profile submit hint. No-cockpit-attached: input parks in the queue and delivers when a cockpit attaches (plugin only delivers to `running` panes it owns). Ordering: FIFO by queue id; `delivered_inputs` + `delivered_at` ack make redelivery idempotent.

Tests: core 147 (incl. queue roundtrip + projection + stopped/unknown rejection), logic 41 (incl. JSONL parse), proxy passthrough, daemon tool-enum coverage — all green; check + clippy (incl. wasm) clean; plugin release rebuilt with the new permission. Needs `just refresh` (V16 + new daemon + new plugin wasm + the proxy is the per-agent binary, so spawned/relaunched agents pick it up) to go live.

Done — all three parts implemented, tested, and clean. The epic #135's last two children (#159, #160) are now complete, so **the entire agent-model epic is finished**.

## Root cause (recap)
The `_mcp-proxy` answered Claude Code's `initialize` locally and **dropped panopt's server `instructions`** (`mcp_proxy.rs` discarded the init body; `handle_initialize` sent none). The agent saw only bare tool descriptions → fell back to its built-in Task tool. Solo connects directly, so its instructions reach the client and claim the verb.

## What I built

**Part 1 — proxy passes instructions through.** `Backend::connect` now captures panoptd's `instructions`; `handle_initialize` includes them. (+2 tests)

**Part 2 — instructions claim the verb.** New "Spawning and tasking agents" section: *use `spawn_agent`, not your built-in sub-agent tool*, for in-project agents; documents `send_input`/`process_stop`.

**Part 3 — ad-hoc spawn + `send_input` (#160):**
- `spawn_agent(prompt, tool_type?, name?)` with no `agent_tool_id` auto-creates a config (cockpit-visible, reuses the whole pipeline) and queues `prompt` as the opening task — so `spawn_agent(prompt="check the weather in Portland")` spawns *and* tasks a child.
- Input queue: `process_inputs` table (V16), `send_input`/`pending_inputs`/`ack_input`, projected to `.panopt/.cockpit/inputs.jsonl`. `send_input` accepts live (`starting`/`running`) instances, rejects stopped/unknown.
- MCP `send_input` (agent-facing) + `input_ack` (cockpit-internal); CLI `_input-ack`.
- Plugin `deliver_pending_inputs` writes into the owned pane via `write_chars_to_pane_id` and acks. **Added the missing `WriteToStdin` permission** (writes would have silently no-op'd otherwise).

## Verification
21 files, ~1190 insertions. Tests: **core 147, logic 41, daemon 5, panopt 171, tool-surface 2** — all green; `just check` + `just clippy` (incl. wasm plugin) clean; plugin release rebuilt. DESIGN.md updated (§10 orchestration surface).

**Not committed.** The working tree holds the uncommitted **#159** work *plus* all of this (they're intertwined — `spawn_agent` grew from `ProcessStartArgs` to `SpawnAgentArgs` as part of ad-hoc spawn). Going live needs **`just refresh`** (V16 migration, new daemon, new plugin wasm; the proxy is per-agent so relaunched/spawned agents pick it up).

Want me to commit? I'd suggest two commits — one for #159 (spawn surface) and one for the proxy-instructions fix + #160 (input channel + ad-hoc spawn) — or a single squashed commit if you prefer. And shall I close the epic **#135**?

1	//! SQLite schema and forward migrations for the persistent store.
2	//!
3	//! One database file holds every project. `todos` and `notes` are keyed
4	//! by `(project_id, id)`, so ids restart at 1 per project and the projected
5	//! files read naturally. The schema version is tracked in SQLite's
6	//! `user_version` pragma so later changes can migrate forward in place.
7	//!
8	//! Note: the `notes` table was called `scratchpads` through V8; the V1-V8
9	//! migration steps below keep that historical name and V9 renames it. Only
10	//! runtime code (and the schema as of V9) speaks of `notes`.
11	
12	use rusqlite::Connection;
13	
14	use crate::agent_profiles::DEFAULT_PROFILE_KEY;
15	
16	/// The current schema version. Bump this and add a step to [`migrate`]
17	/// whenever the schema changes.
18	const SCHEMA_VERSION: i64 = 16;
19	
20	/// Version 1: the initial three-table schema.
21	///
22	/// Per-project id counters live on the `projects` row rather than being
23	/// derived from `MAX(id)`, so a deleted highest todo never causes id reuse.
24	const SCHEMA_V1: &str = "
25	CREATE TABLE projects (
26	    id                 INTEGER PRIMARY KEY,
27	    root               TEXT    NOT NULL UNIQUE,
28	    next_todo_id       INTEGER NOT NULL DEFAULT 1,
29	    next_scratchpad_id INTEGER NOT NULL DEFAULT 1
30	);
31	CREATE TABLE todos (
32	    project_id INTEGER NOT NULL REFERENCES projects(id),
33	    id         INTEGER NOT NULL,
34	    title      TEXT    NOT NULL,
35	    status     TEXT    NOT NULL,
36	    PRIMARY KEY (project_id, id)
37	);
38	CREATE TABLE scratchpads (
39	    project_id INTEGER NOT NULL REFERENCES projects(id),
40	    id         INTEGER NOT NULL,
41	    title      TEXT    NOT NULL,
42	    body       TEXT    NOT NULL,
43	    PRIMARY KEY (project_id, id)
44	);
45	";
46	
47	/// Version 2: the full todo data model (DESIGN.md Section 6.1).
48	///
49	/// Adds the descriptive columns to `todos` and the two side tables that hold a
50	/// todo's comments and its blocked-by relationships, both modeled on Solo's
51	/// schema. The `todo_blockers` table carries a foreign key on each of its two
52	/// todo references, so deleting a todo cascades away the rows where it is the
53	/// blocked todo *and* the rows where it is the blocker. Pre-existing `'done'`
54	/// todos (the only completed value the v1 schema knew) become `'completed'`.
55	const SCHEMA_V2: &str = "
56	ALTER TABLE todos ADD COLUMN body            TEXT    NOT NULL DEFAULT '';
57	ALTER TABLE todos ADD COLUMN priority        TEXT    NOT NULL DEFAULT 'medium';
58	ALTER TABLE todos ADD COLUMN assignee        TEXT    NOT NULL DEFAULT '';
59	ALTER TABLE todos ADD COLUMN tags            TEXT    NOT NULL DEFAULT '[]';
60	ALTER TABLE todos ADD COLUMN created_at      TEXT    NOT NULL DEFAULT '';
61	ALTER TABLE todos ADD COLUMN updated_at      TEXT    NOT NULL DEFAULT '';
62	ALTER TABLE todos ADD COLUMN completed_at    TEXT;
63	ALTER TABLE todos ADD COLUMN next_comment_id INTEGER NOT NULL DEFAULT 1;
64	UPDATE todos SET status = 'completed' WHERE status = 'done';
65	UPDATE todos
66	   SET created_at = datetime('now'), updated_at = datetime('now')
67	 WHERE created_at = '';
68	CREATE TABLE todo_comments (
69	    project_id INTEGER NOT NULL,
70	    todo_id    INTEGER NOT NULL,
71	    id         INTEGER NOT NULL,
72	    author     TEXT    NOT NULL,
73	    body       TEXT    NOT NULL,
74	    created_at TEXT    NOT NULL,
75	    PRIMARY KEY (project_id, todo_id, id),
76	    FOREIGN KEY (project_id, todo_id)
77	        REFERENCES todos(project_id, id) ON DELETE CASCADE
78	);
79	CREATE TABLE todo_blockers (
80	    project_id INTEGER NOT NULL,
81	    todo_id    INTEGER NOT NULL,
82	    blocker_id INTEGER NOT NULL,
83	    PRIMARY KEY (project_id, todo_id, blocker_id),
84	    CHECK (todo_id != blocker_id),
85	    FOREIGN KEY (project_id, todo_id)
86	        REFERENCES todos(project_id, id) ON DELETE CASCADE,
87	    FOREIGN KEY (project_id, blocker_id)
88	        REFERENCES todos(project_id, id) ON DELETE CASCADE
89	);
90	";
91	
92	/// Version 3: the persistent agent/command/terminal roster (todo #67).
93	///
94	/// Adds one `roster` table holding all three kinds, distinguished by a `kind`
95	/// column, modeled on Solo's `processes` table. Like `todos` and `scratchpads`
96	/// it is keyed `(project_id, id)` with a per-project id counter on `projects`.
97	/// Columns are deliberately minimal; per-entry settings (auto-start, env, an
98	/// agent-tool link) are left for later additions.
99	const SCHEMA_V3: &str = "
100	ALTER TABLE projects ADD COLUMN next_roster_id INTEGER NOT NULL DEFAULT 1;
101	CREATE TABLE roster (
102	    project_id   INTEGER NOT NULL REFERENCES projects(id),
103	    id           INTEGER NOT NULL,
104	    kind         TEXT    NOT NULL,
105	    name         TEXT    NOT NULL,
106	    display_name TEXT    NOT NULL DEFAULT '',
107	    command      TEXT    NOT NULL DEFAULT '',
108	    cwd          TEXT    NOT NULL DEFAULT '',
109	    position     INTEGER NOT NULL DEFAULT 0,
110	    created_at   TEXT    NOT NULL,
111	    PRIMARY KEY (project_id, id)
112	);
113	";
114	
115	/// Version 4: timestamps on scratchpads (todo #76).
116	///
117	/// Adds `created_at` and `updated_at` to `scratchpads` so every mutation -
118	/// including append - can bump `updated_at` and the projected index line can
119	/// surface it. That makes the cockpit sidebar visibly refresh on every
120	/// scratchpad change, the same way every todo mutation already changes the
121	/// todo index line through its status/priority fields. The backfill mirrors
122	/// the v1->v2 todo backfill: any pre-existing scratchpad lands with both
123	/// timestamps set to `datetime('now')`.
124	///
125	/// The `ALTER`s run through [`add_column_if_missing`] rather than a raw
126	/// `execute_batch`, so a database stuck at `user_version = 3` whose
127	/// `scratchpads` table already carries the v4 columns - the transitional
128	/// state of any machine that ran an in-development v4 binary before the
129	/// `user_version` bump landed - upgrades cleanly instead of failing on
130	/// "duplicate column name". The backfill is unconditionally safe.
131	fn apply_v4(conn: &Connection) -> Result<(), rusqlite::Error> {
132	    add_column_if_missing(
133	        conn,
134	        "scratchpads",
135	        "created_at",
136	        "TEXT NOT NULL DEFAULT ''",
137	    )?;
138	    add_column_if_missing(
139	        conn,
140	        "scratchpads",
141	        "updated_at",
142	        "TEXT NOT NULL DEFAULT ''",
143	    )?;
144	    conn.execute_batch(
145	        "UPDATE scratchpads
146	            SET created_at = datetime('now'), updated_at = datetime('now')
147	          WHERE created_at = '';",
148	    )
149	}
150	
151	/// Version 5: unify per-resource id counters into one global `next_id` (todo #16).
152	///
153	/// Before V5 every project row carried three independent counters -
154	/// `next_todo_id`, `next_scratchpad_id`, `next_roster_id` - so the same number
155	/// could be handed out as a todo *and* a scratchpad *and* a roster entry. V5
156	/// replaces them with a single `next_id` so a `#N` reference points to exactly
157	/// one resource type forever. Existing rows are left in place: SQLite's
158	/// `(project_id, id)` primary keys are per-table, so any collision in the
159	/// pre-V5 data persists as-is and only the fresh allocations after the
160	/// migration are guaranteed unique.
161	///
162	/// The seed for `next_id` is `max(old three counters)`, which is the lowest
163	/// value safe against every pre-existing id in any of the three tables. The
164	/// three old columns are then dropped.
165	fn apply_v5(conn: &Connection) -> Result<(), rusqlite::Error> {
166	    conn.execute_batch(
167	        "ALTER TABLE projects ADD COLUMN next_id INTEGER NOT NULL DEFAULT 1;
168	         UPDATE projects
169	            SET next_id = MAX(next_todo_id, next_scratchpad_id, next_roster_id);
170	         ALTER TABLE projects DROP COLUMN next_todo_id;
171	         ALTER TABLE projects DROP COLUMN next_scratchpad_id;
172	         ALTER TABLE projects DROP COLUMN next_roster_id;",
173	    )
174	}

agent orchestration: MCP instructions passthrough + input channel (#160)

Fixes why panopt-connected agents spawned their own built-in sub-agent
instead of using panopt, and adds the tasking channel + ad-hoc spawn.

Root cause: _mcp-proxy answered Claude Code's initialize locally and
dropped panoptd's server instructions entirely, so the agent never saw
panopt's guidance - only bare tool descriptions - and fell back to its
built-in Task tool.

- Proxy: capture panoptd's instructions on connect and pass them through
  in the local initialize reply (mcp_proxy.rs).
- Instructions: a "Spawning and tasking agents" section tells the agent to
  use spawn_agent (not its built-in sub-agent tool) for in-project agents,
  and documents send_input / process_stop.
- send_input channel (#160): V16 process_inputs queue; send_input /
  pending_inputs / ack_input in core; projected to .cockpit/inputs.jsonl;
  MCP send_input (agent-facing) + input_ack (cockpit-internal); the plugin
  writes each into the owned pane via write_chars_to_pane_id and acks
  (new WriteToStdin permission; delivered_inputs de-dup). send_input
  requires a live instance, rejecting stopped/unknown with a typed error.
- Ad-hoc spawn: spawn_agent gains tool_type/prompt/name; with no
  agent_tool_id it auto-creates a config and queues prompt as the opening
  input - so spawn_agent(prompt="...") spawns AND tasks a child.

DESIGN §10 already describes this surface. Completes EPIC #135.
EOF
)" && git log --oneline -3
